Design Document (GDD/PRD)

▼

1.0 Project Overview

▼

Territory Grids is a location-based mobile experience that transforms real-world walking into a game of territorial conquest. Players navigate their physical environment to collect virtual dots placed along walkable roads and paths, structured around a global grid system.

1.1 High Concept Pitch

▼

Conceived as 'Pac-Man Geo,' Territory Grids turns every street into a playable level. By walking physical paths, players claim ownership of their neighborhood, transitioning from a simple pedestrian to a territorial conqueror in a parallel digital world.

1.2 Core Gameplay Loop

▼

The core loop consists of: 1. Exploration: Walking in the real world. 2. Collection: Automatically gathering dots within a 4-meter radius. 3. Conquest: Completing 100% of the dots in an S2 Level 15 cell. 4. Expansion: Moving to adjacent cells to grow the player's territory.

2.0 Core Gameplay Mechanics

▼

The gameplay revolves around the intersection of physical movement and digital collection. The system tracks player coordinates in real-time, mapping them to a grid of dots that must be cleared to progress.

2.1 S2 Grid System and Level 15 Units

▼

The game utilizes the S2 geometry library to divide the world into mathematical cells. Level 15 cells are the primary units of play, providing a manageable area for a single walking session while maintaining global consistency.

2.2 Territorial Conquest Requirements

▼

A cell is only considered 'conquered' when every single generated dot within its boundaries has been collected. This 100% requirement ensures players explore every reachable path within a specific territory.

2.3 Single-Player Parallel World Logic

▼

In its initial phase, Territory Grids exists as a single-player 'Parallel World.' Conquests are permanent and local to the player, allowing for an uninterrupted experience of mapping and claiming the world at their own pace.

2.4 Multiplayer Shared World and Clan Mechanics

▼

Future updates will introduce a 'Shared World' (Milestone 5). In this mode, clans will compete for cell ownership. Ownership will be determined by metrics such as 'Speed-to-Conquer' and the number of active members contributing to the territory.

3.0 Dot Generation and Interaction

▼

Dots serve as the primary interactive element. They are programmatically placed to ensure a consistent and safe gameplay experience across diverse geographic locations.

3.1 Programmatic Placement Logic and Intervals

▼

Dots are generated at precise 15-meter intervals along the center-line of walkable paths. This spacing provides a balanced density that rewards steady walking without overwhelming the player or the hardware.

3.2 Path Filtering and Mapbox Attributes

▼

To ensure safety and legality, dot generation is restricted to specific Mapbox attributes: 'pedestrian', 'footway', and 'residential'. This prevents dots from appearing on highways, private property, or restricted zones.

3.3 Boundary and Intersection Logic

▼

To maintain data integrity, dots are not placed within 10 meters of an intersection or an S2 cell boundary. This prevents 'double-counting' dots across multiple cells and ensures a clean visual experience at transitions.

3.4 Collection Radius and Snap-to-Road Mechanics

▼

The player's avatar utilizes 'snap-to-road' functionality to align with Mapbox path data. Any dots within a 4-meter radius of the player's snapped position are automatically collected, allowing for a seamless experience without needing to tap the screen.

4.0 Technical Architecture

▼

The architecture is designed for high performance and offline reliability, ensuring the game remains responsive even in areas with poor cellular connectivity.

4.1 Framework and Tech Stack Overview

▼

The application is built using Flutter for cross-platform compatibility, Mapbox GL for high-fidelity map rendering, and Hive DB for a fast, local-first data storage solution.

4.2 GPS Signal Accuracy and Kalman Filtering

▼

To mitigate GPS drift and variance common in urban environments, a Kalman filter is applied to incoming location data. This ensures the player's avatar moves smoothly and collection remains accurate.

4.3 Movement Validation and Anti-Cheat Integration

▼

To prevent cheating via motorized vehicles, Milestone 3 will integrate native pedometer and step-count data. This validates that the player is moving at walking speeds and physically taking steps to collect dots.

4.4 Offline-First Architecture with Hive DB

▼

Territory Grids prioritizes local storage using Hive DB. This allows players to continue their conquest without an active internet connection, syncing data to the cloud only when a connection becomes available.

5.0 Data Structure and Persistence

▼

Data persistence is optimized for the unique requirements of a location-based game, focusing on minimal storage footprints and rapid lookups.

5.1 S2 Cell ID Indexing

▼

Every S2 cell is indexed in the Hive database using its unique 64-bit S2 Cell ID as the primary key. This allows for near-instantaneous retrieval of cell state as the player moves across the map.

5.2 Bitmask System for Dot Tracking

▼

The collection status of dots within an active cell is stored as a bitmask. This highly efficient format allows the game to track thousands of dots with minimal memory and disk usage.

5.3 Cell State Management (Active vs. Conquered)

▼

Cells exist in two primary states: 'Active' (using bitmasks for dot tracking) and 'Conquered'. Once a cell is 100% complete, the bitmask is purged, and a simple 'isConquered' boolean is set to save space.

5.4 Storage Optimization and Data Pruning

▼

The system includes a 'rubbishing' mechanism that prunes S2 data for territories that are geographically distant from the player's current location, keeping the local database size manageable.

6.0 Resource and Memory Management

▼

To maintain a high frame rate on mobile devices, the game employs aggressive resource management strategies.

6.1 Dynamic Loading Strategy (Depth +1)

▼

The app uses a 'Depth +1' strategy, dynamically loading vector tiles and cell data for the current cell and all immediately adjacent cells. This ensures smooth transitions as the player walks across boundaries.

6.2 Visual Transitions and UI Overlays

▼

When a cell is conquered, the UI triggers a permanent visual overlay change. This provides immediate feedback and a sense of accomplishment, visually marking the player's progress on the map.

6.3 Memory Rubbishing and View Cleanup

▼

As the player moves, old cell data and visual assets are removed from the active view and system memory. This prevents the application's memory footprint from ballooning during long play sessions.

7.0 Roadmap and Future Scalability

▼

The project is structured in phases to ensure the core mechanics are polished before introducing complex multiplayer features.

7.1 Milestone 1: Offline-First Foundation

▼

Focuses on the core engine, Mapbox integration, Hive DB architecture, and the single-player conquest logic in a local-only environment.

7.2 Milestone 3: Health Data Integration

▼

Introduction of health permissions and pedometer data integration to provide a robust anti-cheat layer and validate physical movement.

7.3 Milestone 5: Shared World Migration and Clan Metrics

▼

Transition to a shared world where the Hive 'CellState' objects are extended with 'ConquestMetadata' to track clan ownership and competitive metrics.

7.4 Territory Reset and Historical Tracking

▼

Future updates will allow players to reset conquered territories to earn additional rewards, while maintaining a historical 'times captured' count for each cell.

Pitch Deck

▼

SLIDE 1: Title Slide

Territory Grids: The World is Your Board. Conquer the Grid.

SLIDE 2: The Problem

Most fitness apps are repetitive and location-based games often prioritize complex RPG mechanics over the simple joy of movement. There is a missing link for the 'completionist' walker—someone who wants to gamify their daily commute or neighborhood stroll with a clear, binary sense of accomplishment and territorial ownership.

SLIDE 3: The Solution: Your Project

Territory Grids is a 'Pac-Man Geo' mobile experience that transforms the physical world into a massive, collectible grid. By leveraging S2 geometry, we turn every walkable path into a series of dots. When you collect 100% of the dots in a grid cell, you don't just pass through—you conquer the territory.

SLIDE 4: Core Features & Loop

The gameplay loop is built on 'Walk, Collect, Conquer.' Players navigate real-world paths where dots are programmatically placed every 15 meters. Using a 'snap-to-road' avatar and a 4-meter collection radius, players must clear every single dot within an S2 Level 15 cell to achieve 100% completion. This creates a powerful 'just one more block' psychological drive.

SLIDE 5: Unique Selling Proposition

Unlike other geo-games, Territory Grids uses a hyper-efficient bitmask system for offline-first play, ensuring minimal battery and data drain. Our proprietary filtering logic ensures dots only appear on safe, walkable pedestrian paths, and our '100% or nothing' conquest mechanic offers a more satisfying and definitive goal than traditional area-influence games.

SLIDE 6: Target Audience

Our primary users are 'Urban Completionists'—fitness enthusiasts, daily commuters, and mobile gamers who love tracking progress. We are targeting the multi-billion dollar location-based gaming market, specifically appealing to those who find current offerings too cluttered or combat-focused.

SLIDE 7: Art & Style

The aesthetic is 'Neon-Map Minimalism.' Utilizing Mapbox GL, the game features a sleek dark-mode interface where uncollected paths glow with vibrant dots. Upon conquest, the territory undergoes a permanent visual transformation, washing the grid cell in the player's signature color to signify total dominance.

SLIDE 8: The Team

Our team consists of expert Flutter developers and geospatial engineers specializing in Mapbox integration and high-performance mobile databases. We have a proven track record in building offline-first applications that handle complex coordinate data with precision and speed.

SLIDE 9: The Ask & Roadmap

We are seeking strategic partnerships and funding to accelerate our roadmap. Milestone 1 (Core Engine) is complete. We are now moving toward Milestone 3 (Health/Anti-cheat integration) and Milestone 5, which will introduce the 'Shared World' where clans can compete for global territorial speed-records and ownership.

SLIDE 10: Contact Information

Ready to conquer the grid? Reach out to our lead development team at contact@territorygrids.io or visit territorygrids.io for a live demo of the S2 cell architecture.

MVP Definition

▼

Summary

The Territory Grids MVP focuses on establishing a functional single-player 'Parallel World' experience that validates the core loop of physical movement, programmatic dot collection, and territorial conquest. By prioritizing offline-first local persistence and accurate GPS-to-grid mapping, the launch will demonstrate the feasibility of the 'Pac-Man Geo' concept within S2 Level 15 cells before introducing social or competitive layers.

In Scope

  • ✓ Real-time GPS tracking with Kalman filtering for smooth movement
  • ✓ Mapbox GL integration with snap-to-road functionality
  • ✓ Programmatic dot generation at 15m intervals on pedestrian, footway, and residential paths
  • ✓ Automatic dot collection within a 4m radius of the player
  • ✓ S2 Level 15 grid system for territorial boundaries
  • ✓ 100% dot collection requirement for cell conquest
  • ✓ Local data persistence using Hive DB with bitmask dot tracking
  • ✓ Visual UI overlays to distinguish conquered territories
  • ✓ Depth +1 dynamic loading for seamless cell transitions

Out of Scope

  • ✕ Multiplayer Shared World and Clan ownership mechanics
  • ✕ Pedometer and health data integration for movement validation
  • ✕ Cloud synchronization and global leaderboards
  • ✕ Territory reset mechanics and historical capture counts
  • ✕ Social features and in-game communication
  • ✕ Advanced anti-cheat systems beyond basic GPS validation

MVP Feature Specifications

▼

Real-time GPS tracking with Kalman filtering for smooth movement

▼

User Stories & Criteria

This document outlines the user stories for the Real-time GPS Tracking feature of the Territory Grids project. The primary focus is on utilizing Kalman filtering to provide a smooth, professional user experience by reducing GPS "jitter" and "teleportation."

User Story 1: Smooth Visual Avatar Movement

As a player, I want my map avatar to glide smoothly between GPS updates, So that the movement feels fluid and realistic rather than jumping from point to point.

Description: Standard GPS updates often arrive at irregular intervals (e.g., once per second) and can be off by several meters. This story covers the implementation of the Kalman filter to predict the user's path and provide a continuous stream of coordinates for the UI to render.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Avatar moves fluidly along a path

  • Given the application is open and has a valid GPS lock
  • When the user moves from point A to point B at a steady pace
  • Then the Kalman filter should calculate the predicted velocity and heading
  • And the avatar should move in a continuous linear motion between the raw GPS pings
  • And the visual position should not "snap" or "teleport" more than 0.5 meters during normal movement.

Scenario: Handling a temporary GPS signal loss

  • Given the user is moving and the GPS signal is lost for 2 seconds
  • When the Kalman filter loses new input data
  • Then it should project the user’s position based on the last known velocity for a short grace period
  • And gradually slow the avatar to a stop rather than freezing it instantly.

User Story 2: Mitigation of GPS Jitter (Noise Filtering)

As a Territory Grids user, I want the system to ignore minor "phantom" movements when I am standing still, So that I don't accidentally claim neighboring grid cells while my phone is on a table.

Description: GPS sensors often produce "noise" where the location bounces around even if the device is stationary. This story focuses on the Kalman filter’s ability to weigh the "measurement noise" against the "process noise" to stabilize the position.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Device is stationary with high GPS noise

  • Given the device is physically stationary (e.g., on a desk)
  • When the raw GPS coordinates fluctuate within a 3-meter radius due to atmospheric interference
  • Then the Kalman filter should identify these as low-confidence updates
  • And the filtered coordinate returned to the "Territory Grids" logic should remain static
  • And the user should not be registered as entering a new grid cell.

Scenario: Filtering out high-velocity outliers

  • Given the user is walking at 5 km/h
  • When a single "garbage" GPS ping reports a location 50 meters away (a common GPS spike)
  • Then the Kalman filter should recognize this update as an outlier based on the current state covariance
  • And it should discard or heavily discount that ping, maintaining the user's logical path.

User Story 3: Precise Grid Cell Entry Trigger

As a territory conqueror, I want my entry into a new grid cell to be calculated based on my filtered location, So that I only claim territory that I have actually physically entered.

Description: In "Territory Grids," the logic for capturing a zone depends on the user's coordinates crossing a boundary. Using raw GPS can lead to "false captures." This story ensures the game logic uses the smoothed Kalman output for grid interactions.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Crossing a grid boundary

  • Given the user is 1 meter away from an unclaimed grid cell boundary
  • When the user takes a step across the boundary
  • Then the system should use the Kalman-filtered coordinate to verify the crossing
  • And the "Cell Captured" event should trigger only once the filtered position consistently resides within the new grid coordinates
  • And the UI should highlight the new grid cell immediately upon the filtered coordinate crossing the threshold.

Scenario: Skirting a boundary

  • Given the user is walking exactly parallel to a grid boundary
  • When raw GPS noise occasionally dips into the adjacent cell
  • Then the Kalman filter should maintain the trajectory in the current cell
  • And the system should not trigger a "Cell Entered" event for the adjacent cell unless the filtered heading shows a clear intent to enter.

Technical Specifications

This technical specification outlines the implementation of a Kalman Filter-based GPS tracking system for the Territory Grids project. The goal is to transform noisy, irregular GPS pings into a smooth, high-fidelity movement stream suitable for real-time gaming and precise territorial conquest.

Data Model

The following data structures define the raw input from the hardware and the internal state of the Kalman Filter.

Field Type Description
timestamp integer Epoch time in milliseconds when the coordinate was recorded.
latitude double Raw or filtered latitude in decimal degrees.
longitude double Raw or filtered longitude in decimal degrees.
accuracy double Horizontal accuracy of the location in meters (used as measurement noise).
velocity_x double Calculated longitudinal velocity (meters per second).
velocity_y double Calculated latitudinal velocity (meters per second).
variance_p double Process variance (internal uncertainty of the model).
variance_m double Measurement variance (uncertainty of the GPS hardware).
covariance_matrix list A 4x4 matrix representing the state uncertainty (Lat, Lon, V_lat, V_lon).

Game State

The system must maintain a persistent "Filtered State" in memory to ensure continuity between GPS pings.

State Variable Type Description
current_filtered_pos object The most recent (Lat, Lon) output from the Kalman Filter.
last_raw_ping object The last raw coordinate received from the GPS hardware for outlier comparison.
movement_status enum Current state: STATIONARY, WALKING, or SIGNAL_LOST.
prediction_buffer list A queue of projected coordinates used for 60fps UI interpolation.
grace_period_timer integer Countdown in milliseconds since the last valid GPS update.
active_s2_cell_id string The S2 Level 15 Cell ID the user is currently occupying based on filtered data.

API / Local Service Interfaces

Since this is an offline-first MVP, the "API" refers to the internal Location Service interface.

Method Parameters Return Type Description
initializeFilter initial_lat, initial_lon void Sets the starting state of the Kalman Filter.
processGpsUpdate raw_location_data filtered_coordinate Ingests a raw ping, runs the filter, and returns the smoothed point.
getInterpolatedPos current_frame_time coordinate Returns a predicted position for the UI to render between pings.
resetFilter void void Clears covariance matrices; used when the user teleports (e.g., app restart).

Key Components

  1. GPS Stream Provider: A wrapper for the platform-specific location API (CoreLocation for iOS / Google Play Services for Android). It normalizes incoming data and handles permission states.
  2. Kalman Engine: The mathematical core. It performs the "Predict" and "Update" phases. It uses the GPS accuracy value to dynamically adjust the measurement noise matrix ($R$).
  3. Outlier Detector: A pre-filter component that compares incoming pings against the current state covariance. If a ping is $>3$ standard deviations from the predicted position, it is flagged as "garbage" and discarded or heavily discounted.
  4. UI Interpolator: A high-frequency ticker (60Hz) that moves the map avatar. It doesn't wait for GPS pings; it moves the avatar toward the Kalman-predicted position using linear interpolation (lerp).
  5. Grid Trigger Manager: Monitors the filtered coordinate. When the coordinate crosses an S2 Level 15 boundary, it verifies the "dwell time" (to ensure it's not a noise spike) and triggers the Cell Captured event.

Logic Flow

1. The Kalman Cycle

The filter operates in two distinct phases:

  • Prediction Phase: Whenever the UI requests a frame (60fps) or a new GPS ping arrives, the filter projects the state forward in time:
    • $NewPosition = OldPosition + (Velocity * \Delta t)$
    • Uncertainty (Covariance) increases over time as we move away from the last known measurement.
  • Update Phase: When a raw GPS ping arrives:
    • Calculate the Kalman Gain (how much to trust the new ping vs. the prediction).
    • If the ping has high accuracy (low meters), the Gain is high.
    • Adjust the position and velocity based on the difference between the prediction and the actual ping.
    • Shrink the Uncertainty (Covariance) because we now have a new measurement.

2. Handling Stationary Jitter

To prevent "phantom movement" (User Story 2):

  • If the calculated velocity falls below a threshold (e.g., 0.2 m/s), the filter enters Stationary Mode.
  • In this mode, the Process Noise ($Q$) is significantly reduced, making the filter highly resistant to changing the position unless a series of high-confidence pings indicate a clear departure.

3. Grace Period for Signal Loss

  • If no GPS ping is received for $>1.0$ seconds, the Kalman Engine continues to provide predicted coordinates based on the last known velocity.
  • The MovementSmoother applies a friction coefficient to the velocity, gradually slowing the avatar to a stop over 3 seconds to prevent "infinite walking" through walls during a tunnel or signal drop.

Implementation Logic: Kalman Update Step

// Simplified 1D representation (applied to Lat and Lon independently for MVP)
function update(measurement, accuracy) {
    // 1. Prediction
    predicted_pos = last_estimate + velocity * time_delta;
    predicted_variance = last_variance + process_noise;

    // 2. Outlier Detection
    if (abs(measurement - predicted_pos) > (3 * sqrt(predicted_variance))) {
        return last_estimate; // Ignore outlier
    }

    // 3. Update
    kalman_gain = predicted_variance / (predicted_variance + accuracy);
    current_estimate = predicted_pos + kalman_gain * (measurement - predicted_pos);
    current_variance = (1 - kalman_gain) * predicted_variance;

    // 4. Velocity Update
    velocity = (current_estimate - last_estimate) / time_delta;
    
    return current_estimate;
}

Dependencies

  • S2 Geometry Library: Required for mapping the filtered coordinates to Level 15 grid cells.
  • Mapbox GL SDK: The rendering engine for the avatar and grid overlays.
  • Device Motion (Optional/Future): Accelerometer data can be added to the Kalman Filter (Sensor Fusion) in later iterations to improve dead reckoning.
  • Hive DB: To persist the last known "good" location so the app opens where the user left off.

Mapbox GL integration with snap-to-road functionality

▼

User Stories & Criteria

Project: Territory Grids

Feature: Mapbox GL Integration with Snap-to-Road Functionality

This feature aims to provide users with the ability to create precise territory boundaries that automatically align with the existing road network provided by Mapbox GL. This ensures that territory definitions are logical, follow real-world infrastructure, and eliminate "dead zones" caused by imprecise freehand drawing.

User Story 1: Precise Territory Drawing with Road Snapping

As a Territory Manager,
I want the map cursor to automatically snap to the nearest road when I am drawing a territory boundary,
So that my grids are perfectly aligned with street centerlines and logical geographic dividers.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Drawing a new territory boundary with snapping enabled

  • Given I am in the "Create Territory" mode
  • And the "Snap to Road" toggle is set to ON
  • When I click on the map within 20 pixels of a recognized road segment
  • Then the vertex of the polygon should be placed exactly on the road's centerline
  • And the visual line connecting to the previous vertex should follow the shortest path along the road network (where applicable)

Scenario: Visual feedback for snapping

  • Given I am moving my cursor over the Mapbox GL map
  • And the "Snap to Road" toggle is ON
  • When my cursor hovers near a road
  • Then a visual "snap indicator" (e.g., a small circle or highlight) should appear on the nearest road segment to show where the point will land.

User Story 2: Toggle Snapping for Freeform Flexibility

As a GIS Analyst,
I want the ability to toggle the "Snap to Road" functionality on and off,
So that I can draw boundaries across parks, water, or rural areas where roads do not exist or are not the desired boundary.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Disabling snapping for off-road boundaries

  • Given I am drawing a territory boundary
  • When I toggle "Snap to Road" to OFF
  • And I click on a location that is not on a road (e.g., a forest or a lake)
  • Then the vertex should be placed exactly at the cursor's coordinates without jumping to the nearest road.

Scenario: Switching modes mid-draw

  • Given I have already placed three vertices with "Snap to Road" enabled
  • When I toggle "Snap to Road" to OFF and place a fourth vertex
  • Then the first three vertices should remain snapped to their original road positions
  • And the fourth vertex should be placed exactly where I clicked.

User Story 3: Snapping During Vertex Manipulation

As a Territory Manager,
I want existing territory vertices to snap to the road network when I drag them to new locations,
So that I can quickly update and refine territory shapes while maintaining geographic precision.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Adjusting an existing boundary vertex

  • Given an existing territory polygon is displayed on the map
  • And I am in "Edit Mode" with "Snap to Road" enabled
  • When I click and drag an existing vertex toward a different street
  • Then the vertex should snap to the centerline of the new street as soon as it enters the snapping threshold (e.g., 20 pixels)
  • And the area calculation for the territory should update in real-time based on the new snapped coordinates.

Scenario: Snapping to intersections

  • Given I am dragging a vertex near the meeting point of two roads
  • When the vertex is within the snapping threshold of an intersection
  • Then the vertex should snap precisely to the center of the intersection point.

Technical Specifications

Technical Specification: Mapbox GL Snap-to-Road Integration

This document outlines the technical requirements and implementation strategy for the "Snap-to-Road" functionality within the Territory Grids project. This system ensures that territory boundaries align with real-world infrastructure using Mapbox GL vector tile data and spatial analysis.

1. Data Model

The following table defines the data structures required to support territory creation and snapping persistence.

Field Type Description
territory_id String Unique UUID for the territory polygon.
boundary_points List Ordered list of Lat/Lng coordinates defining the polygon.
snap_metadata List Metadata for each vertex indicating if it is snapped and the associated Road ID.
is_closed Boolean Whether the polygon has been completed (last point matches first).
area_sq_meters Double The calculated surface area of the territory.
parent_s2_cell String The S2 Level 15 cell ID where this territory is anchored.
road_segment_ids List Collection of Mapbox/OSM IDs for road segments used as boundaries.

2. Game State

The application must track the following state variables to manage the drawing and editing lifecycle.

Variable Type Description
is_snap_enabled Boolean Global toggle determining if snapping logic is active.
interaction_mode Enum Current state: IDLE, DRAWING, EDITING.
hovered_road_point LatLng | null The calculated snap target currently under the user's cursor.
active_vertex_index Integer | null The index of the vertex currently being dragged in EDITING mode.
snapping_threshold_px Integer The pixel distance (default 20) within which snapping triggers.
current_polygon_geojson Object Live GeoJSON representation of the territory being drawn.

3. API Endpoints (Mapbox Integration)

While Mapbox GL handles most visual tasks client-side, the following Mapbox Web Services are utilized for precision snapping and pathfinding.

Route Method Payload Description
Mapbox Tilequery API GET /v4/mapbox.mapbox-streets-v8/tilequery/{lon},{lat}.json?radius=20&layers=road Retrieves road geometry features within the pixel threshold.
Mapbox Map Matching API POST { "coordinates": [[lon,lat], [lon,lat]], "profile": "walking" } Snaps a series of points to the most logical road path between them.

4. Key Components

SnapProvider

A utility class responsible for querying the Mapbox Map instance. It uses map.queryRenderedFeatures to find 'road' layers within the snapping radius and calculates the nearest point on that line geometry.

TerritoryDrawingEngine

The core controller managing the drawing lifecycle. It listens to map click events, manages the boundary_points array, and triggers the snapping logic before updating the state.

SnapIndicator (UI)

A visual layer (Mapbox Source + Layer) that renders a "ghost" point or highlight on the nearest road segment when hovered_road_point is not null.

GeometryCalculator

A service using Turf.js to perform real-time area calculations and distance checks. It ensures that the territory remains valid (no self-intersection) while snapping.

5. Logic Flow

A. Snap-to-Road Calculation (Real-time Hover)

  1. Listen for mousemove on the Mapbox canvas.
  2. If is_snap_enabled is false, exit.
  3. Convert cursor screen coordinates to a bounding box (e.g., 20px x 20px).
  4. Query Mapbox GL features: map.queryRenderedFeatures(bbox, { layers: ['road-label', 'road-simple'] }).
  5. If features are found:
    • Identify the closest road segment.
    • Use Turf.js nearestPointOnLine to find the exact coordinate on the road centerline.
    • Update hovered_road_point state.
  6. If no features are found, set hovered_road_point to null.

B. Vertex Placement

  1. On click event:
    • If hovered_road_point is active, append those coordinates to boundary_points.
    • If hovered_road_point is null, append the raw cursor coordinates.
  2. If boundary_points.length > 1 and Snap is ON:
    • (Optional) Call Map Matching API to get the geometry of the road between the previous vertex and the current vertex to ensure the line follows the curve of the street.

C. Vertex Manipulation (Edit Mode)

  1. User selects a vertex (index i).
  2. As the user drags, the Snap-to-Road Calculation (Logic Flow A) runs continuously.
  3. The boundary_points[i] is updated to the hovered_road_point if within threshold.
  4. The area_sq_meters is recalculated using turf.area() and updated in the UI.

6. Implementation Logic (Snapping Algorithm)

/**
 * Logic to determine the snap point based on cursor position
 * Used by SnapProvider
 */
function getSnappedCoordinate(e, map, threshold) {
  const bbox = [
    [e.point.x - threshold, e.point.y - threshold],
    [e.point.y + threshold, e.point.y + threshold]
  ];

  // Query road layers from Mapbox Vector Tiles
  const features = map.queryRenderedFeatures(bbox, {
    layers: ['road-street', 'road-primary', 'road-secondary', 'road-intersection']
  });

  if (!features.length) return null;

  let closestPoint = null;
  let minDistance = Infinity;

  features.forEach(feature => {
    // Use Turf.js to find the closest point on the line geometry
    const snapped = turf.nearestPointOnLine(feature, turf.point([e.lngLat.lng, e.lngLat.lat]));
    const distance = snapped.properties.dist;

    if (distance < minDistance) {
      minDistance = distance;
      closestPoint = snapped.geometry.coordinates;
    }
  });

  return closestPoint;
}

7. Dependencies

  • Mapbox GL JS/SDK: Primary map engine and vector tile source.
  • Turf.js: Required for spatial operations (nearestPointOnLine, area, booleanIntersects).
  • S2 Geometry Library: Required for mapping snapped territories to S2 Level 15 cells for the "Territory Grid" logic.
  • Hive DB: For local persistence of draft polygons and snap metadata (Offline-first requirement).

Programmatic dot generation at 15m intervals on pedestrian, footway, and residential paths

▼

User Stories & Criteria

This document outlines the user stories and Gherkin-style acceptance criteria for the Territory Grids feature, specifically focusing on the programmatic generation of waypoints (dots) at 15-meter intervals.

User Story 1: Automated Waypoint Generation

As a GIS Data Specialist,
I want the system to automatically calculate and place waypoints at 15-meter intervals along the centerline of mapped paths,
So that I have a standardized, granular grid for territory coverage analysis without manual plotting.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Successfully generating dots on a standard path segment

  • Given a valid polyline representing a path segment
  • And the total length of the path is 45 meters
  • When the programmatic dot generation process is triggered
  • Then the system should place exactly 4 dots (0m, 15m, 30m, and 45m)
  • And each dot must be snapped precisely to the path geometry.

Scenario: Handling path segments shorter than the interval

  • Given a path segment that is 10 meters long
  • When the programmatic dot generation process is triggered
  • Then the system should place a dot at the start point (0m) and the end point (10m)
  • And no 15m interval dot should be created.

User Story 2: Path Type Filtering & Classification

As a Territory Planner,
I want the dot generation to be restricted to specific OpenStreetMap (OSM) tags (pedestrian, footway, and residential),
So that our field teams are not assigned waypoints on high-speed motorways or inaccessible private industrial roads.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Validating dots on allowed path types

  • Given a map area containing a "residential" street and a "motorway"
  • When the generation script runs for that area
  • Then dots should be generated at 15m intervals along the "residential" street
  • But no dots should be generated on the "motorway" segment.

Scenario: Inclusion of footways and pedestrian paths

  • Given a park area mapped with "footway" and "pedestrian" tags
  • When the generation script runs
  • Then the system must identify these segments as valid targets
  • And generate dots at the 15m interval across the entire length of these paths.

User Story 3: Dot Metadata and Coordinate Precision

As a Field Operations Manager,
I want each generated dot to carry unique identifiers and precise GPS coordinates,
So that I can export the grid to mobile navigation apps and track completion status for every specific point.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Verifying dot attributes and uniqueness

  • Given a successfully generated grid of dots
  • When I inspect the metadata of an individual dot
  • Then it should contain a unique Point_ID
  • And it should include the Latitude and Longitude in decimal degrees (6 decimal places)
  • And it should include the Path_Type attribute (e.g., "residential") from which it was generated.

Scenario: Handling path intersections

  • Given an intersection where a "footway" meets a "residential" path
  • When the dots are generated for both paths
  • Then the system should ensure that overlapping dots at the exact same coordinate are deduplicated into a single waypoint to prevent double-counting.

Technical Notes for Implementation:

  • Interval Calculation: Use a "Great Circle" or "Haversine" formula to ensure 15m accuracy regardless of global latitude.
  • Data Source: Integration with OpenStreetMap (OSM) or internal GeoJSON layers is required.
  • Performance: The generation should be optimized for batch processing (e.g., processing a 5km² area in under 30 seconds).

Technical Specifications

This technical specification outlines the implementation of the Programmatic Dot Generation system for the Territory Grids MVP. The system is designed to transform OpenStreetMap (OSM) linear features into a discrete grid of collectible waypoints while maintaining high spatial accuracy and performance.

1. Data Model

The following schema defines the structure for individual waypoints (dots) and their relationship to the S2 grid system.

Field Type Description
point_id String Unique identifier (UUID or Hash of coordinates) for the dot.
latitude Double GPS Latitude coordinate, stored at 6 decimal places.
longitude Double GPS Longitude coordinate, stored at 6 decimal places.
path_type String The OSM source tag (e.g., "residential", "footway", "pedestrian").
s2_cell_id String The S2 Level 15 Cell ID containing this point.
bit_index Integer The unique index of this dot within its S2 Cell bitmask (0-N).
is_collected Boolean Local flag indicating if the player has captured this dot.
parent_way_id Long The original OSM Way ID from which the dot was generated.

2. Game State

The game state manages the lifecycle of dots within the viewport and tracks player progress locally.

Variable Type Description
active_dot_pool List The set of dots currently loaded into memory for the player's vicinity.
conquered_cell_ids Set Collection of S2 Level 15 IDs where collection is 100%.
cell_bitmask_cache Map<String, Bitset> Map of S2 Cell IDs to bitmasks representing collected dots.
generation_queue Queue S2 Cell IDs pending dot generation/processing.
is_generating Boolean Global flag to prevent concurrent generation processes.

3. API & Service Interface

While the MVP focuses on local persistence, the following internal service interfaces are required for data orchestration.

Service/Route Method Parameters Description
OSM_Fetch GET Bounding Box (S2 Cell) Retrieves GeoJSON/OSM data for specific path types.
Dot_Generator Internal Geometry, Interval (15m) Logic to interpolate points along a polyline.
Persistence_Sync Local (Hive) S2_Cell_ID, Bitmask Saves current collection progress to local storage.
Grid_Validator Internal List Deduplicates dots at intersections and assigns bit indices.

4. Key Components

  • S2CellManager: Responsible for calculating the current player cell and identifying the "Depth +1" neighbors that require data pre-loading.
  • PathFilterEngine: A utility that parses OSM data and discards any geometry not tagged as residential, footway, or pedestrian.
  • DotInterpolator: The core logic component that traverses polylines and calculates coordinates at exactly 15m intervals using Haversine math.
  • SpatialDeduplicator: A post-processing module that identifies dots within a 0.5m radius of each other (common at intersections) and merges them into a single Point_ID.
  • BitmaskRegistry: Maps Point_IDs to a fixed integer index per S2 cell to allow for extremely lightweight persistence in Hive DB.

5. Logic Flow: Dot Generation Algorithm

The generation process occurs when a player enters a new S2 Level 15 cell that has not been previously initialized.

  1. Trigger: Player moves within range of an uninitialized S2 Level 15 cell.
  2. Fetch: Retrieve polyline data for the cell's bounding box filtering for highway=residential|footway|pedestrian.
  3. Interpolate: For each segment in a polyline:
    • Place a dot at distance = 0.
    • Calculate the segment length ($L$).
    • While current_distance + 15m <= L, place a dot at current_distance + 15m.
    • Place a final dot at distance = L (the end of the segment).
  4. Snap & Clean:
    • Round all coordinates to 6 decimal places.
    • Check for existing dots in the active_dot_pool within a 0.5m threshold. If a match is found, discard the new dot to handle intersections.
  5. Index: Sort all unique dots in the cell (e.g., by Longitude then Latitude) and assign each a bit_index from 0 to $N-1$.
  6. Persist: Save the generated dot definitions and an empty Bitset (all 0s) to Hive DB.

Implementation Logic (Pseudo-code)

void generateDotsForPath(Polyline path, String type) {
  double pathLength = calculateHaversineLength(path);
  double currentDist = 0.0;

  // Always add start point
  addDot(path.points.first, type);

  while (currentDist + 15.0 < pathLength) {
    currentDist += 15.0;
    Point interpolatedPoint = interpolateAlongPath(path, currentDist);
    addDot(interpolatedPoint, type);
  }

  // Always add end point
  addDot(path.points.last, type);
}

6. Dependencies

  • S2 Geometry Library: For cell boundary calculation and indexing.
  • Mapbox GL / Overpass API: Source for real-world path geometries.
  • Geodesy/LatLong Library: For accurate Haversine distance and interpolation calculations.
  • Hive DB: For high-speed local storage of bitmasks and dot metadata.
  • Kalman Filter: (Pre-requisite) To ensure player position is stable before checking dot collection radius.

Automatic dot collection within a 4m radius of the player

▼

User Stories & Criteria

Feature: Automatic Dot Collection (Territory Grids)

In the Territory Grids project, this feature aims to improve the user experience by removing the need for manual interaction with every individual grid point. By implementing a proximity-based collection system, players can focus on movement and exploration while the system handles the data/resource gathering.

User Story 1: Proximity-Based Automatic Collection

As a Player
I want dots to be automatically collected when I am within a 4-meter radius of them
So that I can focus on my physical surroundings and movement without having to manually tap the screen for every point.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Player moves within range of a single dot

  • Given I am logged into the Territory Grids app
  • And there is an uncollected dot at coordinates (X, Y)
  • When my GPS location moves to within 4 meters of (X, Y)
  • Then the dot should be marked as "Collected" in the database
  • And the dot should disappear or change state on my map view

Scenario: Player is outside the collection radius

  • Given there is an uncollected dot 5 meters away from my current position
  • When I remain at my current position
  • Then the dot should remain "Uncollected"
  • And no interaction should be triggered

User Story 2: Feedback and Reward Logic

As a Player
I want to receive immediate visual and haptic feedback when a dot is automatically collected
So that I am aware of my progress and rewards without needing to constantly stare at my phone screen.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Visual and Haptic confirmation of collection

  • Given I am walking through a territory with dots
  • When a dot is automatically collected via the 4m radius trigger
  • Then I should feel a short haptic vibration (if enabled)
  • And my "Total Dots Collected" counter should increment by 1 in the UI
  • And a brief "fly-out" animation should show the dot moving toward my score indicator

Scenario: Collection during background play

  • Given the app is running in the foreground but my screen is dimmed
  • When I enter the 4m radius of a dot
  • Then the system should still process the collection and update my account balance

User Story 3: Handling Multiple Dots in Dense Areas

As a Player
I want the system to efficiently collect all dots within the 4-meter radius simultaneously
So that I don't miss any points when walking through a high-density grid area.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario: Multiple dots within the 4m radius

  • Given there are 3 uncollected dots within a 4-meter radius of my current location
  • When my location update is processed by the app
  • Then all 3 dots should be collected in a single batch operation
  • And my total score should increase by 3
  • And the UI should display a single consolidated feedback message (e.g., "+3 Dots Collected") to avoid screen clutter

Scenario: Rapid movement through a grid

  • Given I am moving at a walking pace (approx. 1.4 m/s)
  • When the proximity check runs (at a defined polling interval)
  • Then the system must calculate the distance for all nearby dots to ensure none are skipped due to latency between GPS pings.

Technical Specifications

This technical specification outlines the implementation of the Automatic Dot Collection system for the Territory Grids project. The focus is on high-performance proximity detection using S2 geometry and efficient local state management via bitmasks.

Data Model

The system uses a highly optimized bitmask approach within Hive DB to track dot collection. This avoids the overhead of managing thousands of individual database rows for every coordinate.

Field Type Description
cellId String The unique S2 Level 15 cell token representing the territory.
dotsBitmask List A byte array/list of integers where each bit represents a dot's status (0: Available, 1: Collected).
totalDots int The total number of dots generated for this cell based on road/path geometry.
collectedCount int The current number of bits set to 1 in the bitmask.
isConquered boolean Calculated flag: True if collectedCount equals totalDots.
dotCoordinates List A cached list of the physical coordinates for dots in this cell, indexed to match the bitmask.
lastSyncTimestamp long Unix timestamp of the last time this cell's state was pushed to the server.

Game State

The active game state is managed in-memory to ensure the proximity engine can run at high frequencies (e.g., every 500ms-1s) without UI lag.

Variable Name Type Description
currentPosition LatLng The latest smoothed GPS coordinate after Kalman filtering.
activeDotsPool Map<int, Dot> A collection of uncollected dots from the current and adjacent (Depth +1) S2 cells.
proximityRadius double Constant set to 4.0 (meters).
sessionBatchCount int Temporary counter for dots collected in the current proximity check to drive consolidated UI feedback.
isHapticEnabled boolean User preference toggle for vibration feedback.
lastProcessedLocation LatLng The coordinate of the last proximity check used to prevent redundant calculations if the player is stationary.

API Endpoints

While the MVP focuses on local persistence, the following endpoints are required for account-level synchronization and global territory ownership.

Route Method Payload / Description
/v1/territory/sync POST { "cellId": string, "bitmask": string } - Synchronizes local collection progress to the cloud.
/v1/territory/claim POST { "cellId": string, "playerId": string } - Triggered when a bitmask is 100% filled to grant ownership.
/v1/dots/generate GET ?cellId=string - Returns the list of generated dot coordinates for a specific S2 cell based on OpenStreetMap data.

Key Components / Classes

  1. LocationProcessor: Responsible for receiving raw GPS streams, applying Kalman filtering, and snapping the player position to the Mapbox road network.
  2. ProximityEngine: The core logic handler. It calculates the distance between the currentPosition and all dots in the activeDotsPool.
  3. BitmaskManager: A utility class that performs bitwise operations to update the collection status and calculate the collectedCount.
  4. CollectionManager: Orchestrates the workflow: updates the database, triggers the FeedbackService, and checks for cell conquest.
  5. FeedbackService: Manages the UI/UX layer, including the fly-out animations and haptic triggers via the device's vibration hardware.

Logic Flow

The proximity check must be efficient to prevent battery drain while maintaining accuracy.

  1. Input: Receive a filtered GPS update (Target frequency: 1Hz).
  2. Delta Check: If the distance between currentPosition and lastProcessedLocation is < 0.5 meters, abort the check to save resources.
  3. Spatial Query:
    • Identify the current S2 Level 15 cell.
    • Retrieve uncollected dots for the current cell and 8 surrounding neighbors (Depth +1).
  4. Distance Calculation:
    • Iterate through the activeDotsPool.
    • Calculate the distance using the Haversine formula (or a simplified Euclidean approximation for short distances).
  5. Batch Collection:
    • Identify all dots where distance <= 4.0m.
    • Update the dotsBitmask for each identified dot by setting the bit at the dot's index to 1.
  6. Persistence & UI:
    • Write the updated bitmask to Hive DB.
    • Trigger a single haptic pulse if batchCount > 0.
    • Pass the batchCount to the UI to display a consolidated "+X Dots" message.
    • Execute the fly-out animation for each collected dot coordinate.
  7. Conquest Check: If collectedCount == totalDots, trigger the Territory Conquest event.

Dependencies

  • S2 Geometry Library: For mapping GPS coordinates to Level 15 cell IDs and identifying neighbor cells.
  • Hive DB: For high-speed local NoSQL storage of bitmasks.
  • Kalman Filter Plugin: To smooth erratic GPS signals and prevent "teleporting" collection.
  • Mapbox GL: For rendering the grid overlays and handling the dot fly-out animations.
  • Haptics API: Native device access for tactile feedback.
  • OpenStreetMap (OSM) Data: Required by the dot generation logic to ensure dots are placed on traversable paths.

S2 Level 15 grid system for territorial boundaries

▼

User Stories & Criteria

This document outlines the core user stories for the Territory Grids project, specifically focusing on the implementation of the S2 Level 15 grid system.

S2 Level 15 cells provide a highly granular grid (approximately 150m x 150m at the equator), making them ideal for precise territorial management, urban planning, or location-based service zones.

User Story 1: Grid Visualization and Overlay

As a Territory Manager, I want to see an S2 Level 15 grid overlay on the map, so that I can visually understand the boundaries of the cells and how they align with physical landmarks.

Description: The map interface should render the S2 Level 15 grid lines dynamically as the user zooms in. To maintain performance, the grid should only render at appropriate zoom levels (e.g., Zoom Level 14 and higher).

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Rendering the grid at high zoom levels

  • Given I am viewing the territory map
  • And I have zoomed in to level 15 or higher
  • When the map finishes loading
  • Then I should see a semi-transparent grid overlay representing S2 Level 15 cells
  • And each cell should be clearly outlined.

Scenario: Hiding the grid at low zoom levels for performance

  • Given I am viewing the territory map with the S2 grid visible
  • When I zoom out to level 12 or lower
  • Then the S2 grid overlay should be hidden to prevent visual clutter and performance degradation.

User Story 2: Territory Definition via Cell Selection

As a Territory Planner, I want to select individual or multiple S2 cells to define a "Territory," so that I can assign specific business rules or personnel to a precise geographic area.

Description: Users need a way to group these 150m cells into a named "Territory." The system must store the unique S2 Cell IDs (64-bit integers or hex strings) associated with that territory record.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Selecting a single cell to view details

  • Given the S2 grid is visible on the map
  • When I click on a specific cell
  • Then the cell should be highlighted
  • And the system should display the unique S2 Cell ID for that specific grid square.

Scenario: Creating a new territory from multiple cells

  • Given I am in "Edit Territory" mode
  • When I click on five different S2 cells and click "Save"
  • Then the system should create a new Territory record
  • And it should store the 5 unique S2 Cell IDs in the database associated with that Territory name.

User Story 3: Coordinate-to-Cell Resolution API

As a System Developer, I want an API endpoint that converts Latitude/Longitude coordinates into an S2 Level 15 Cell ID, so that the system can automatically determine which territory a user or asset is currently in.

Description: This is the backend logic that powers the "Point-in-Polygon" check using S2 geometry. Instead of heavy spatial joins, the system should simply calculate the S2 ID of a coordinate and check for a match in the Territory database.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Successfully resolving a coordinate to a cell

  • Given a valid set of GPS coordinates (e.g., 40.7128, -74.0060)
  • When I send a request to the /resolve-cell API endpoint
  • Then the system should return the S2 Level 15 Cell ID (e.g., 89c25a17...)
  • And the response time should be under 50ms.

Scenario: Identifying territory membership

  • Given a coordinate that falls within a previously defined "Downtown" territory
  • When the system processes the S2 Level 15 cell for that coordinate
  • Then the API should return the name of the territory ("Downtown") associated with that cell ID.

Technical Notes for the Team:

  • S2 Library: We will use the Google S2 Geometry library (available in C++, Java, Python, and Go).
  • Precision: At Level 15, the average area of a cell is roughly 0.0225 km².
  • Storage: S2 Cell IDs should be stored as unsigned 64-bit integers (uint64) for maximum indexing performance in the database.

Technical Specifications

This technical specification outlines the implementation of the S2 Level 15 grid system for the Territory Grids project. This system serves as the spatial foundation for territorial boundaries, player progression, and the "Pac-Man Geo" core loop.

1. Data Model

The following data structures define how S2 cells and territories are persisted. We use 64-bit unsigned integers for S2 Cell IDs to ensure high-performance indexing and compatibility with the Google S2 library.

Field Type Description
cell_id uint64 The unique S2 Level 15 identifier (stored as a string in some DBs for precision).
territory_id UUID Foreign key linking the cell to a specific named Territory group.
status Enum Current state of the cell: unclaimed, in_progress, or conquered.
dot_mask Blob/Bitset A bitmask representing the collection status of programmatic dots within the cell.
total_dots Integer The total number of dots generated for this specific cell based on path density.
collected_dots Integer Counter for dots collected; used to trigger conquest when it equals total_dots.
conquered_at Timestamp The date and time the cell status changed to conquered.
last_visited Timestamp The last time the player's GPS coordinates fell within this cell.

2. Game State

The game state tracks the player's real-time interaction with the grid and manages the UI/UX transitions between different territories.

Variable Type Description
current_cell_id uint64 The S2 Cell ID where the player is currently located.
active_territory_id UUID The ID of the territory the player is currently inside (if any).
visible_cells List A collection of S2 Cell IDs currently within the map's viewport.
selection_buffer Set Temporary storage for cells selected by the user in "Edit Territory" mode.
is_grid_visible Boolean Toggle state for the S2 grid overlay based on map zoom level.
conquest_progress Float Percentage (0.0 to 1.0) of dots collected in the current_cell_id.

3. API Endpoints

While the MVP focuses on local persistence (Hive DB), the following internal API structure (or local service methods) is required for coordinate resolution and territory management.

Route Method Payload Description
/resolve-cell POST { lat: float, lng: float } Converts coordinates to an S2 Level 15 Cell ID.
/territory/lookup GET ?cell_id=uint64 Returns territory metadata associated with a specific cell.
/territory/create POST { name: string, cells: uint64[] } Groups multiple S2 cells into a named Territory.
/cell/status GET ?cell_id=uint64 Returns dot collection progress and conquest status for a cell.

4. Key Components

  • S2GeometryProvider: A wrapper service for the Google S2 Geometry library. It handles coordinate-to-cell conversion and calculates cell boundary coordinates (lat/lng vertices) for map rendering.
  • GridOverlayLayer: A custom Mapbox GL layer responsible for drawing the S2 grid lines. It listens to map zoom events and toggles visibility at Zoom Level 14+.
  • ConquestManager: The business logic engine that monitors dot_mask updates. When a mask is full (100% collection), it triggers the state change from in_progress to conquered.
  • SpatialIndexService: Manages the local Hive DB. It optimizes queries to find "neighboring" cells (Depth +1) to ensure seamless loading as the player moves.

5. Logic Flow

A. Grid Rendering & Visibility

  1. Zoom Monitor: The UI listens to the Mapbox onCameraMove event.
  2. Threshold Check: If zoom >= 14.0, calculate the current Map Bounding Box (Viewport).
  3. Cell Generation: Pass the Bounding Box to S2GeometryProvider.getCellsInRegion(level: 15).
  4. GeoJSON Conversion: Convert the resulting S2 Cell IDs into a GeoJSON FeatureCollection where each feature is a polygon representing the cell's four vertices.
  5. Render: Update the GridOverlayLayer source with the new GeoJSON.

B. Coordinate-to-Cell Resolution

  1. Input: Receive raw GPS signal (filtered via Kalman Filter).
  2. S2 Conversion: 
    S2LatLng latLng = S2LatLng::FromDegrees(lat, lng);
S2CellId cellId = S2CellId::FromLatLng(latLng).parent(15);
  3. State Update: If the resulting cellId differs from current_cell_id, trigger a "Cell Transition" event.
  4. Data Fetch: Load the dot_mask and status for the new cell from Hive DB.

C. Territory Conquest Logic

  1. Movement: Player moves within 4m of a dot coordinate.
  2. Bitmask Update: Set the bit corresponding to that dot index in the dot_mask to 1.
  3. Completion Check: Compare collected_dots count to total_dots.
  4. Conquest Trigger: If 100%, update status to conquered and trigger a UI notification/visual change (e.g., cell fill color changes to the player's team color).

6. Dependencies

  • Google S2 Geometry Library: Core library for spherical geometry and hierarchical cell decomposition.
  • Mapbox GL SDK: For map rendering and custom layer support.
  • Hive DB: For high-speed, local NoSQL storage of cell states and bitmasks.
  • GPS/Kalman Filter Module: Required to provide stable coordinates to the S2 resolution logic.
  • Dot Generation Engine: Must provide the fixed dot coordinates for each S2 cell based on OpenStreetMap (OSM) path data.

100% dot collection requirement for cell conquest

▼

User Stories & Criteria

Project: Territory Grids

Feature: 100% Dot Collection Requirement for Cell Conquest

This feature implements a strict "all-or-nothing" mechanic for territory acquisition. To claim a grid cell, a player must successfully collect every collectible "dot" within that specific cell's boundaries.

User Story 1: Core Conquest Logic

As a player, I want the grid cell to transition to my ownership only after I have collected every dot within its boundaries, so that there is a clear and challenging requirement for expanding my territory.

Business Value: Ensures gameplay depth by preventing "drive-by" captures and requiring players to fully engage with the content of a cell before gaining the strategic advantage of ownership.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin):

Scenario: Successfully conquering a cell

  • Given I am in a neutral grid cell that contains 10 dots
  • And I have already collected 9 dots
  • When I collect the 10th and final dot
  • Then the cell status should change from "Neutral" to "Captured"
  • And the cell color should change to my player color
  • And I should receive a "Cell Conquered" notification

Scenario: Failing to conquer with partial collection

  • Given I am in a neutral grid cell that contains 10 dots
  • When I collect 5 dots and move to an adjacent cell
  • Then the original cell status should remain "Neutral"
  • And the ownership should not transfer to me

User Story 2: Progress Visualization & Feedback

As a player, I want to see a real-time counter or progress bar of dots collected within my current cell, so that I know exactly how much work is left to complete the conquest.

Business Value: Improves player retention and reduces frustration by providing clear goals and visual feedback on their proximity to success.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin):

Scenario: Updating progress UI upon collection

  • Given I am inside a cell with a total of 20 dots
  • And the UI shows "0/20 Dots Collected"
  • When I collect 1 dot
  • Then the UI should immediately update to show "1/20 Dots Collected"
  • And a progress bar should reflect 5% completion

Scenario: Visualizing 100% completion

  • Given I have collected 19 out of 20 dots
  • When I collect the final dot
  • Then the progress UI should highlight (e.g., glow or change color) to indicate 100% completion
  • And the counter should be replaced by a "Captured" icon

User Story 3: Persistence of Partial Progress

As a player, I want my dot collection progress to be saved if I leave a cell and return later, so that I don't lose my effort if I need to retreat or explore elsewhere before finishing a conquest.

Business Value: Supports non-linear gameplay and prevents player burnout by respecting the time invested in difficult or large grid cells.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin):

Scenario: Returning to a partially cleared cell

  • Given I am in "Cell A" which has 50 dots
  • And I collect 25 dots
  • When I exit "Cell A" and enter "Cell B"
  • And I later return to "Cell A"
  • Then the cell should still show 25/50 dots collected
  • And the 25 dots I previously collected should not have respawned

Scenario: Completing a previously abandoned cell

  • Given I have returned to "Cell A" with 25/50 dots remaining
  • When I collect the remaining 25 dots
  • Then the 100% conquest logic should trigger
  • And I should gain ownership of the cell as per standard rules

Technical Specifications

This technical specification outlines the implementation of the "100% Dot Collection" mechanic for the Territory Grids MVP. The system ensures that territory conquest is an all-or-nothing achievement, utilizing S2 Level 15 cells and local persistence for offline-first reliability.

Data Model

The data model is designed for high-performance lookups and efficient storage of dot collection states using bitmasks. This data is persisted locally via Hive DB.

Field Type Description
cell_id String Unique S2 Level 15 cell token.
total_dots Integer The total number of dots programmatically generated within the cell boundaries.
collected_mask String A bitmask (stored as a hex string) where each bit represents the collection status of a dot.
collected_count Integer Cached count of bits set to 1 in the collected_mask for quick UI updates.
status String Current state of the cell: 'Neutral' or 'Captured'.
owner_id String Unique ID of the player who conquered the cell (null if status is 'Neutral').
last_updated Timestamp ISO 8601 string of the last time a dot was collected or status changed.

Game State

The runtime game state tracks the player's immediate interaction with their current grid environment.

Variable Type Description
active_cell_id String The S2 token of the cell currently occupied by the player's GPS coordinates.
current_progress_pct Float Calculated value (collected_count / total_dots) used for the progress bar UI.
nearby_dots_buffer List A list of dot objects (ID, Lat, Lng) within the active and adjacent cells (+1 depth).
is_conquest_pending Boolean True if collected_count == total_dots but the "Captured" animation/notification hasn't finished.

API Endpoints (Internal Service Layer)

Since the MVP is offline-first, these "endpoints" represent the methods provided by the GridRepository and ConquestService.

Method Target Payload Description
GET /cell/{cell_id} None Retrieves the current collection status and bitmask for a specific cell.
POST /cell/{cell_id}/collect { dot_index: int } Updates the bitmask, increments count, and checks for 100% completion.
POST /cell/{cell_id}/conquer { player_id: string } Transitions cell status to 'Captured' and assigns ownership.
GET /sync/status None (Future) Returns a list of cell_ids and masks to sync with the cloud.

Key Components / Classes

  1. S2GridProvider: Responsible for converting GPS coordinates into S2 Level 15 tokens and calculating the bounding boxes for dot generation.
  2. DotGenerator: A deterministic service that generates dot coordinates at 15m intervals along OpenStreetMap (OSM) pathways within a cell.
  3. CollectionEngine: Monitors the distance between the player's filtered GPS position and the nearby_dots_buffer. Triggers collection when distance < 4m.
  4. ConquestManager: The logic gatekeeper that evaluates the collected_count == total_dots condition and triggers the ownership state change.
  5. PersistenceService (Hive): Handles the low-level CRUD operations for the bitmasks and cell statuses to ensure progress is saved if the app closes.
  6. ProgressUIController: A reactive controller that updates the "X/Y Dots Collected" text and the progress bar smoothing.

Logic Flow

1. Dot Collection & Progress Tracking

  1. GPS Update: The app receives a Kalman-filtered GPS coordinate.
  2. Cell Check: Determine if the player is in a new cell_id. If yes, load the bitmask from Hive.
  3. Proximity Detection:
    • Iterate through dots in the active_cell_id where the bitmask value is 0.
    • Calculate distance. If distance $\le$ 4.0 meters:
      • Set bit at dot_index to 1.
      • Increment collected_count.
      • Save updated bitmask to Hive.
  4. UI Update: Emit the new collected_count to the UI stream to update the progress bar and counter.

2. Conquest Evaluation

  1. Immediately following a collection, the ConquestManager compares collected_count to total_dots.
  2. Condition Met: If collected_count == total_dots:
    • Set status to 'Captured'.
    • Set owner_id to CurrentPlayer.id.
    • Trigger "Cell Conquered" event.
  3. Visual Feedback:
    • Change Mapbox layer filter to style the cell polygon with the player's color.
    • Replace progress UI with the "Captured" icon.
    • Trigger haptic feedback and overlay notification.

3. Persistence & Re-entry

  1. When a player exits a cell, the collected_mask remains stored in Hive.
  2. Upon re-entering the cell (detected via S2 token change), the GET /cell/{cell_id} logic retrieves the existing mask.
  3. The DotGenerator recreates the dots, but the CollectionEngine ignores those marked as 1 in the mask, preventing respawning.

Dependencies

  • S2 Geometry Library: For grid calculation and token generation.
  • Hive DB: For local, high-speed NoSQL storage of bitmasks.
  • Mapbox GL SDK: For rendering the grid overlays and handling polygon color changes.
  • Kalman Filter Implementation: To prevent "GPS jump" from accidentally collecting dots or triggering cell entries.
  • Geolocator: For high-accuracy background/foreground location updates.

Local data persistence using Hive DB with bitmask dot tracking

▼

User Stories & Criteria

Project: Territory Grids

Feature: Local Data Persistence using Hive DB with Bitmask Dot Tracking

This feature focuses on implementing a high-performance local storage solution to track which "dots" or "cells" within a territory grid have been visited or activated. By using Hive DB (a lightweight NoSQL database) and Bitmasking, we ensure that even large grids (thousands of points) can be stored and retrieved with minimal memory overhead and disk space.

User Story 1: Persisting Grid Progress Locally

As a Territory Explorer, I want my grid progress to be automatically saved to my device, So that I don't lose my visited "dots" when I close the app or lose internet connectivity.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Successfully saving a visited dot to Hive

  • Given I am viewing a territory grid
  • And the Hive "territory_box" is successfully initialized
  • When I visit a specific dot within a grid sector
  • Then the application should calculate the new bitmask for that sector
  • And the updated bitmask should be persisted to the Hive database using the sector ID as the key
  • And the save operation should be performed asynchronously to prevent UI jank.

Scenario: Handling database write failures

  • Given the device storage is full or Hive is inaccessible
  • When the system attempts to save an updated bitmask
  • Then the system should log a persistence error
  • And the user should see a non-intrusive notification that "Progress is currently not being saved."

User Story 2: Efficient State Tracking via Bitmasks

As a System Architect, I want to store grid cell states as bitmask integers rather than individual boolean records, So that the database footprint remains small and the read/write speeds remain near-instant.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Converting grid cell states to a bitmask for storage

  • Given a grid sector containing 64 individual dots
  • When the state of these dots changes (e.g., dot at index 5 is toggled)
  • Then the system should represent this state as a 64-bit integer (bitmask)
  • And only this single integer should be sent to the Hive DB for storage
  • And the database should not store individual coordinate objects for every dot.

Scenario: Validating bitmask integrity on retrieval

  • Given a stored bitmask integer in Hive for Sector "A1"
  • When the application requests the data for Sector "A1"
  • Then the system should perform a bitwise comparison to map the bits back to the visual grid dots
  • And the UI must accurately reflect the "visited" status for every bit set to 1 in the mask.

User Story 3: Seamless Session Restoration

As a Returning User, I want the app to instantly load my previous territory progress upon startup, So that I can continue my exploration exactly where I left off.

Acceptance Criteria:

Scenario: Restoring grid state on app launch

  • Given I have previously visited several dots in multiple sectors
  • When I launch the "Territory Grids" application
  • Then the system should open the Hive "territory_box" during the splash screen/initialization phase
  • And it should fetch all stored bitmasks for the current map view
  • And the grid should render with the correct dots highlighted based on the retrieved bitmasks within < 200ms.

Scenario: Initializing a new grid with no history

  • Given I am a new user or have cleared my data
  • When I open a territory grid for the first time
  • Then Hive should return a null or default value for the bitmasks
  • And the application should initialize a "zeroed-out" bitmask (all bits set to 0)
  • And the UI should display a completely empty/unvisited grid.

Technical Specifications

Technical Specifications: Local Data Persistence with Bitmasking

This document outlines the technical implementation for persisting territory grid progress using Hive DB and bitmasking. This approach optimizes for high-performance updates and minimal storage footprint.

1. Data Model

The persistence layer uses a Key-Value approach where the Key is the unique S2 Cell identifier and the Value is a compact object containing the bitmask and metadata.

Field Type Description
sectorId String Unique identifier for the S2 Level 15 cell (e.g., "89c259b").
dotMask Integer (64-bit) A bitmask representing 64 dots. 1 = Visited, 0 = Unvisited.
lastUpdated Integer Unix timestamp of the last time a dot was collected in this sector.
isConquered Boolean Flag indicating if all bits in the mask are set to 1.
syncStatus String Status for future cloud sync (e.g., "synced", "pending").

2. Game State

The application state must maintain a reactive map of the currently loaded sectors to ensure the UI updates instantly when a bitmask changes.

State Variable Type Description
loadedSectors Map<String, SectorData> In-memory cache of sectors currently visible on the map or in adjacent buffers.
activeSectorId String The ID of the S2 cell the player is currently physically inside.
persistenceError String? Holds error messages if Hive writes fail (used for UI notifications).
isInitializing Boolean True while Hive boxes are being opened during app splash screen.
totalDotsCollected Integer Global counter of all bits set to 1 across all stored sectors.

3. API / Repository Interface (Local)

While this feature is local-first, the repository pattern will be used to abstract Hive operations.

Method Parameters Return Type Description
getSectorMask sectorId: String Future Retrieves the 64-bit mask for a specific sector. Returns 0 if not found.
saveSectorMask sectorId: String, mask: Integer Future Persists the updated mask to the "territory_box".
getAllConqueredSectors None Future<List> Returns a list of Sector IDs where isConquered is true.
clearLocalData None Future Wipes the Hive box for testing or data reset.

4. Key Components & Classes

Persistence Manager (HiveService)

Responsible for the lifecycle of the Hive database. It handles box encryption (if required), path initialization, and graceful closing.

Bitmask Logic Engine

A utility class that performs bitwise operations. It maps a specific dot's local index (0-63) to a bit position.

  • Operation: currentMask | (1 << dotIndex) to set a bit.
  • Operation: (currentMask >> dotIndex) & 1 to check a bit.

Sector Repository

The bridge between the UI/Game Logic and Hive. It handles the conversion between raw Hive data and the SectorData domain model.

Conquest Listener

A background service that monitors bitmask updates. When a mask reaches the value 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (all 64 bits set), it triggers the "Territory Conquered" event.

5. Logic Flow

A. Dot Collection & Persistence

  1. Input: Player enters a 4m radius of a dot coordinate.
  2. Mapping: The system identifies the sectorId (S2 Cell) and the dotIndex (0-63) based on the dot's relative position in the grid.
  3. Read: The current bitmask for that sectorId is pulled from the loadedSectors state.
  4. Bitwise Update: A bitwise OR operation is performed: newMask = oldMask | (1 << dotIndex).
  5. State Update: The loadedSectors map is updated with the newMask, triggering a UI repaint (dot changes color).
  6. Async Write: The newMask is sent to HiveService.saveSectorMask(sectorId, newMask).
  7. Error Handling: If the write fails, the persistenceError state is updated to trigger a non-intrusive notification.

B. Session Restoration

  1. Init: On app launch, Hive.openBox('territory_box') is called.
  2. Fetch: The system identifies the user's last known GPS location.
  3. Buffer Load: The system queries Hive for the sectorId at that location plus all adjacent sectors (Depth +1).
  4. Hydration: The loadedSectors state is populated with these values.
  5. Render: The Mapbox overlay draws the grid, using the bitmask to determine which dots to render as "collected."

6. Implementation Logic (Bitmask Example)

// Example of bitmask manipulation for a 64-dot grid
class BitmaskCalculator {
  // Sets a specific dot to 'visited'
  static int setDotVisited(int currentMask, int dotIndex) {
    if (dotIndex < 0 || dotIndex > 63) return currentMask;
    return currentMask | (1 << dotIndex);
  }

  // Checks if a specific dot has been visited
  static bool isDotVisited(int currentMask, int dotIndex) {
    return (currentMask & (1 << dotIndex)) != 0;
  }

  // Checks if all 64 dots are collected
  static bool isSectorComplete(int currentMask) {
    // 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF represents 64 bits set to 1
    return currentMask == -1; // In Dart, bitwise representation of all 1s in a 64-bit signed int is -1
  }
}

7. Dependencies

  • Hive DB: For high-performance NoSQL local storage.
  • S2 Geometry Library: To calculate Sector IDs from GPS coordinates.
  • Location Service: To provide real-time GPS coordinates for dot-proximity checks.
  • Path Generation Engine: To provide the static list of 64 dot coordinates per S2 cell that the bitmask maps to.

Visual UI overlays to distinguish conquered territories

▼

User Stories & Criteria

This document outlines the user stories and acceptance criteria for the Visual UI Overlays feature within the Territory Grids project. The goal is to provide players with clear, real-time visual feedback regarding land ownership and faction boundaries.

User Story 1: Color-Coded Ownership Overlays

As a Player
I want each grid cell to be tinted with a semi-transparent color representing the faction that owns it
So that I can instantly distinguish between my territory, allied territory, and enemy territory at a glance.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin)

Scenario: Visualizing ownership on the map

  • Given the player is viewing the main tactical map
  • And "Faction A" owns a specific set of grid cells
  • When the map renders the territory layer
  • Then all cells owned by "Faction A" should display a semi-transparent blue overlay
  • And all cells owned by "Faction B" should display a semi-transparent red overlay
  • And neutral cells should have no color overlay (remain transparent)

Scenario: Maintaining visibility of underlying terrain

  • Given a grid cell has a color overlay applied
  • When the player looks at the cell
  • Then the underlying terrain features (e.g., mountains, forests, roads) must still be visible through the overlay
  • And the overlay opacity should be set to 30% by default

User Story 2: Real-time Capture Feedback

As a Player
I want the visual overlay of a grid cell to update immediately when its ownership status changes
So that I receive instant confirmation that my conquest or loss has been registered by the game.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin)

Scenario: Successfully capturing an enemy cell

  • Given the player is attacking an enemy-controlled cell (Red overlay)
  • When the player’s units successfully conquer the cell
  • Then the red overlay should immediately disappear
  • And a blue overlay (Player faction) should fade in over the cell within 500ms
  • And a brief "border pulse" animation should trigger to highlight the change

Scenario: Losing a cell to an opponent

  • Given the player owns a cell (Blue overlay)
  • When an enemy faction successfully captures that cell
  • Then the blue overlay should be removed
  • And the cell should be tinted with the enemy's color (Red overlay)

User Story 3: Territory Boundary Lines

As a Strategic Player
I want thick, high-contrast borders to appear at the edges where two different factions meet
So that I can clearly see the "front lines" of a conflict even when zoomed out.

Acceptance Criteria (Gherkin)

Scenario: Rendering borders between factions

  • Given a grid cell owned by "Faction A" is adjacent to a cell owned by "Faction B"
  • When the map is rendered
  • Then a solid, 2px wide border line should be drawn on the edge shared by those two cells
  • And the color of the border should be a brighter, opaque version of the owning faction's color

Scenario: Removing borders for contiguous territory

  • Given two adjacent cells are owned by the same faction
  • When the map is rendered
  • Then no border line should be drawn between those two specific cells
  • And they should appear as one continuous "blob" of faction color

Scenario: Toggling the overlay for clarity

  • Given the player is in a "Scouting Mode"
  • When the player presses the "Toggle UI Overlays" hotkey (e.g., 'V')
  • Then all color tints and boundary lines should be hidden to show the raw terrain
  • And pressing the hotkey again should restore the ownership visuals to their previous state

Technical Specifications

This technical specification details the implementation of visual overlays for the Territory Grids project, focusing on S2 Level 15 cell rendering, faction-based color coding, and dynamic boundary calculations using Mapbox GL and local Hive DB persistence.

1. Data Model

The following data structures define how territory ownership is stored locally. This data is used to drive the rendering engine.

Field Type Description
cellToken String The S2 Level 15 hex token representing the grid cell.
